question: So does a Signal block an unsafe answer before the user receives it, or is that something my agent must do separately?

conversation_context.content: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

I reached this turn's research limit without a draft passing all checks. Research may be incomplete, or the verifier may have rejected a useful draft; this does not establish that the docs lack an answer. Inspect the trace for the stopping reason.

answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the docs I read, a Signal doesn't block anything. Your agent has to do the blocking itself, and Weave documents a separate guardrails feature for that.

**What Signals do**
- Signals score your agent's turns. They apply tags such as `nsfw` or `user-frustration`, or ratings from 0 to 1, to matching spans. [S11]
- Their stated purpose is to "surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention." [S1]
- The Signals tab is a table of scored turns, with a score, a trend and a time for each row. [S12]
- The agent Signals pages I read describe flagging and reviewing. They don't describe stopping a response before it is delivered.

**What blocks a response**
- Weave's guardrails page says guardrails use inline Weave Scorers to assess user input or LLM output and "adjust the LLM's responses in real time". They run before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores cross thresholds. [S9] [S10]
- Guardrails "require code changes because they affect your application's control flow." [S10] You call the scorer in your own code and decide what to return, for example a fallback message.
- The guardrails page contrasts guardrails with monitors, which score traffic passively without changing your application's control flow. [S10]
- Guardrail scorer results are stored automatically in Weave, so they also work as monitors. [S10]
- The guardrails page is about Weave Scorers. It does not describe agent Signals, so I haven't treated the two as one pipeline.

**Practical takeaway**
- If you need an unsafe answer stopped before the user sees it, put a scorer check in your agent's code path.
- Use Signals alongside that check to review, trend and investigate flagged turns after they happen.

**Limit of my research:** I didn't find a documented Signals setting that blocks or rewrites responses. That only covers the pages I read, so it doesn't prove no such feature exists.

sources.title: Monitor your agents with signals
sources.heading: Create a new signal
sources.text:
## Create a new signal

To start scoring your agent's turns, create one or more signals. Select **+ New signal** to open the **Create signals** drawer.

The drawer groups available signals into two categories:

* **Tags**: Apply a label automatically to matching spans, such as `user-frustration` or `nsfw`. Use tags to categorize spans or flag unwanted behavior. The signals UI only displays rows for spans that matched at least one tag, so a tag signal might run successfully even if you don't see any output.
* **Ratings**: Assign a score from 0 to 1 to matching spans. Use ratings to rate agent performance and measure improvements over time.

sources.title: Monitor your agents with signals
sources.heading: Signals table
sources.text:
## Signals table

The Signals tab displays a table of scored turns from your agent. Each row represents the output of one of your signal monitors. The following columns appear by default.

| Column | Description |
| - | - |
| **Type** | The part of the conversation that gets scored. Only `turn` is supported. |
| **Scorer** | The name of the signal that produced this score. |
| **Last message** | A preview of the last message in the scored turn, with the role shown below. |
| **Agent** | The agent associated with the scored turn. |
| **Scores** | The numeric rating from 0.0 to 1.0, or a tag if matched. We recommend using consistent ratings where 1 indicates good and 0 indicates bad, but your scorers can use any scale you define. |
| **Trend** | Displays an inline chart that shows how this signal trends over time. Shows either the average value (for ratings) or the count (for tags). |
| **When** | When the signal was scored. |

Use the time window selector and **Filter** bar to narrow results by scorer, agent, score range, or time period. The **Score volume** timeline shows counts of signals that Weave evaluated for ratings or tagged. It reflects the rows shown in the table and supports drag-to-filter on the timeline.

sources.heading: Set up guardrails
sources.text:
# Set up guardrails

> Ensure LLM safety and measure output quality in production applications

Guardrails intervene in your LLM application's behavior based on scores from LLM judges. They run in real time before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores exceed thresholds. You can use guardrails to block toxic content, filter responses for personally identifiable information (PII), or block abusive input from users.

This guide explains how Weave guardrails work, how to tune their performance, and walks through examples that use built-in scorers, custom scorers, and AWS Bedrock Guardrails to protect production LLM applications.

sources.heading: How Weave guardrails work
sources.text:
## How Weave guardrails work

Weave guardrails use inline [Weave Scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md) to assess the input from a user or the output from an LLM and adjust the LLM's responses in real time. You can configure custom scorers or use [built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) to assess content for a variety of purposes. This guide demonstrates how to use both types of scorers as guardrails.

If you want to passively score production traffic without modifying your application's control flow, use [monitors](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md) instead.

Unlike monitors, guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. However, every scorer result from guardrails is automatically stored in Weave's database, so your guardrails also function as monitors without any extra configuration. You can analyze historical scorer results regardless of how they were originally used.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools required to set up guardrails.

# Set up guardrails

> Ensure LLM safety and measure output quality in production applications

Guardrails intervene in your LLM application's behavior based on scores from LLM judges. They run in real time before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores exceed thresholds. You can use guardrails to block toxic content, filter responses for personally identifiable information (PII), or block abusive input from users.

This guide explains how Weave guardrails work, how to tune their performance, and walks through examples that use built-in scorers, custom scorers, and AWS Bedrock Guardrails to protect production LLM applications.

result.heading: How Weave guardrails work
result.text:
## How Weave guardrails work

Weave guardrails use inline [Weave Scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md) to assess the input from a user or the output from an LLM and adjust the LLM's responses in real time. You can configure custom scorers or use [built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) to assess content for a variety of purposes. This guide demonstrates how to use both types of scorers as guardrails.

If you want to passively score production traffic without modifying your application's control flow, use [monitors](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md) instead.

Unlike monitors, guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. However, every scorer result from guardrails is automatically stored in Weave's database, so your guardrails also function as monitors without any extra configuration. You can analyze historical scorer results regardless of how they were originally used.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools required to set up guardrails.

input.answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the docs I read, a Signal doesn't block anything. Your agent has to do the blocking itself, and Weave documents a separate guardrails feature for that.

**What Signals do**
- Signals score your agent's turns. They apply tags such as `nsfw` or `user-frustration`, or ratings from 0 to 1, to matching spans. [S11]
- Their stated purpose is to "surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention." [S1]
- The Signals tab is a table of scored turns, with a score, a trend and a time for each row. [S12]
- The agent Signals pages I read describe flagging and reviewing. They don't describe stopping a response before it is delivered.

**What blocks a response**
- Weave's guardrails page says guardrails use inline Weave Scorers to assess user input or LLM output and "adjust the LLM's responses in real time". They run before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores cross thresholds. [S9] [S10]
- Guardrails "require code changes because they affect your application's control flow." [S10] You call the scorer in your own code and decide what to return, for example a fallback message.
- The guardrails page contrasts guardrails with monitors, which score traffic passively without changing your application's control flow. [S10]
- Guardrail scorer results are stored automatically in Weave, so they also work as monitors. [S10]
- The guardrails page is about Weave Scorers. It does not describe agent Signals, so I haven't treated the two as one pipeline.

**Practical takeaway**
- If you need an unsafe answer stopped before the user sees it, put a scorer check in your agent's code path.
- Use Signals alongside that check to review, trend and investigate flagged turns after they happen.

**Limit of my research:** I didn't find a documented Signals setting that blocks or rewrites responses. That only covers the pages I read, so it doesn't prove no such feature exists.

Calls count application invocations, not every HTTP attempt. This is not an invoice. Research counts do not measure factual completeness.
